Articles contributing to recommendations were reviewed
based on specified inclusion and exclusion criteria, with the
goal of identifying evidence relevant to physical therapists’
clinical decision making for individuals with CTS. The title
and abstract of each article were reviewed independently
by 2 members of the CPG development group for inclusion
(see APPENDIX B for inclusion and exclusion criteria). Full-text
review was then similarly conducted. A third member of
the CPG development group provided the final decision on
discrepancies that were not resolved by the initial reviewers
(see APPENDIX C for the flowchart of articles). Data extraction
and assignment of level of evidence were also performed by
2 members of the CPG development group. Evidence tables
for this CPG are available on the Clinical Practice Guidelines
page of the APTA Orthopedics website (www.orthopt.org).
This guideline was issued in 2026 based on the published
literature through May 12, 2025, and will be considered for
review by the CPG development group in 2031, or sooner if
new evidence becomes available. Any updates to the guideline in the interim period will be noted on the APTA Orthopedics website (www.orthopt.org).

LEVELS OF EVIDENCE
Individual clinical research articles were graded according to
criteria adapted from the Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine,
Oxford, United Kingdom, for diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic studies. In teams of 2, each reviewer independently
evaluated the quality of each article using a critical appraisal
tool and assigned a level of evidence. See APPENDICES D and E for
the Levels of Evidence table and details on procedures used for
assigning levels of evidence, available at www.orthopt.org. The
evidence update was organized from the highest level of evidence to the lowest level. An abbreviated version of the grading
system is provided in TABLE 1.

STRENGTH OF EVIDENCE AND GRADES OF RECOMMENDATION
The strength of the evidence supporting the recommendations was graded according to the established methods

TABLE 1
Levels of Evidence

I
Evidence obtained from high-quality diagnostic studies, prospective

studies, systematic reviews, or randomized controlled trials

II
Evidence obtained from lesser-quality diagnostic studies, systematic

reviews, prospective studies, or randomized controlled trials (eg, weaker
diagnostic criteria and reference standards, improper randomization, no
blinding, less than 80% follow-up)

III
Case-control studies or retrospective studies

IV
Case series

V
Expert opinion

provided in TABLE 2. Two members of the CPG development group developed recommendations based on the
strength of evidence, including how directly the studies
addressed the questions relating to CTS. In developing
recommendations, the group considered the strengths
and limitations of the body of evidence and the health
benefits, side effects, and risks of tests and interventions.
All members of the CPG development group voted on the
recommendations.

GUIDELINE REVIEW PROCESS AND VALIDATION
Identified reviewers who are experts in management and
rehabilitation of CTS or upper extremity rehabilitation reviewed this CPG content and methods for integrity, accuracy, and that it fully represents the condition. In addition,
reviewers were invited from a panel including consumer/

Some patients need diagnostic testing, and EDX testing remains a reference standard regardless of its limitations. Recent evidence on the use of diagnostic US in individuals with
signs and symptoms of CTS has provided useful information
on nerve morphology.

PAIN SEVERITY
Many patients who develop CTS have classic signs and symptoms as previously described, but there is evidence that pain
is prevalent, and can negatively impact quality of life. In a
recent study, 39.2% of patients with CTS reported pain >
4/10.40 Individuals with painful CTS had lower quality of life
scores on the 36-item Short Form Survey (SF-36) compared
to those with nonpainful CTS in the following domains:
physical functioning, role limitations due to physical health,
bodily pain, and perceived health change (P<.05).40 The most
significant predictors of pain intensity among people with
CTS are increased compound motor action potential latency,
presence of night pain, and thenar weakness.149

In a sample of 108 individuals with CTS, 80% had neuropathic pain, and of these, 63% were classified as having mild
pain and 37% were classified as having moderate or severe
pain measured by the Douleur Neuropathique 4 questionnaire.127 The Douleur Neuropathique 4 questionnaire is a
screening tool used to identify the presence of neuropathic pain.24 Neuropathic pain was associated with increased
symptom duration, higher scores on the Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire Symptom Severity Scale (BCTQ-SSS) and
Functional Status Scale (BCTQ-FSS), reduced pinprick and
light touch sensations, insomnia severity, pain catastrophizing, pain anxiety, and spread of symptoms outside the median
nerve distribution.127

chunks.text:
CENTRAL PAIN MECHANISMS
Extramedian spread of symptoms, defined as spread of
symptoms outside the median nerve distribution, is often
interpreted as a sign of central sensitization.167 Central sensitization is defined as the increased responsiveness of nociceptive neurons in the central nervous system to their normal or
subthreshold afferent input.84 A recent systematic review and
meta-analysis identified low- to moderate-certainty evidence
suggesting altered brain structure and function in individuals
with chronic CTS.166

It should be noted there is no reference standard for measuring central sensitivity in a clinical setting. Pressure pain
threshold, temporal summation, and conditioned pain modulation have been used as proxy measures in recent high-quality
studies, but when comparing results from individuals with
CTS to control groups, findings are conflicting.125, 126, 140,167 The
Central Sensitization Inventory is a self-report questionnaire
used to quantify central sensitivity symptoms in other chronic

pain conditions.159 However, scores on the questionnaire did
not correlate to pressure pain threshold, temporal summation, or conditioned pain modulation in patients with CTS.
There was a stronger relationship between Central Sensitization Inventory scores and depression than proxy measures
of central sensitivity.125 While the clinical course for some
patients with CTS may include extramedian spread of symptoms, confirmation and clinical measurement of central pain
mechanisms are limited.

chunks.text:
PSYCHOSOCIAL FACTORS
Psychosocial factors have become an area of interest in CTS.
Approximately 30% of people with CTS have anxiety and depression,145 and women show worse depression scores than
men.146 Studies on the association between psychosocial factors and CTS are conflicting. Sun et al169 found psychological distress, pain catastrophizing, and illness perceptions
accounted for 20% of the variance in the BCTQ-FSS and
25% of the variance in the BCTQ-SSS. Papadopoulou et al146
found moderate correlations between BCTQ scores and depression and anxiety (r = 0.49 and 0.45, respectively), but
coefficient values were not statistically significant (P = .052
and .084, respectively). Fernández-de-las-Peñas et al63 found
no relationship between psychosocial factors and the extent
or spread of pain measured using a pain diagram. There are
no studies examining the association of psychosocial factors
and outcomes following nonsurgical management of CTS.
Núñez-Cortés et al136 reported that physical activity had a
positive impact on pain and depression in individuals with
CTS. High levels of self-reported physical activity resulted
in lower pain intensity (12.41 mm) and lower depressive
symptoms (3.29 points). Psychosocial factors may impact
outcome following CTR.100,137 According to a systematic review, anxiety and depression were associated with symptom
severity; anxiety was associated with return to work; and depression was associated with functional impairments, pain,
and patient satisfaction after CTR. Pain catastrophizing was
also associated with functional impairments and return to
work.137 Kennedy et al100 reported pain-related worry, anxiety, and functional interference were also associated with
poor surgical outcome. Núñez-Cortés et al137 suggested
screening patients to identify individuals at risk for an unfavorable outcome.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING AND CLASSIFICATION
There is currently no reference standard for diagnosis of CTS,
which makes diagnostic confirmation challenging.20,105 Some
patients will undergo EDX testing or diagnostic US, and in
some cases, findings will alter their course of treatment.
Electrodiagnostic testing provides an objective measure of
myelinated nerve fiber function relative to other nerves in
the hand and may differentiate CTS from other compression
neuropathies or nerve injuries. It provides measurements

cpg10 | april 2026 | volume 56 | number 4 | journal of orthopaedic & sports physical therapy

of focal demyelination and axonal loss.22 Electrodiagnostic
testing does not detect abnormalities in small, unmyelinated
nerve fiber function (C and A-δ), which are mediators of pain,
nor does it record sensory action potentials perceived by the
patient as paresthesia.22

Núñez-Cortés et al
reported that physical activity had a
positive impact on pain and depression in individuals with
CTS. High levels of self-reported physical activity resulted
in lower pain intensity (12.41 mm) and lower depressive
symptoms (3.29 points). Psychosocial factors may impact
outcome following CTR.
According to a systematic re-
view, anxiety and depression were associated with symptom
severity; anxiety was associated with return to work; and de-
pression was associated with functional impairments, pain,
and patient satisfaction after CTR. Pain catastrophizing was
also associated with functional impairments and return to
work.
Kennedy et al
reported pain-related worry, anx-
iety, and functional interference were also associated with
poor surgical outcome. Núñez-Cortés et al
suggested
screening patients to identify individuals at risk for an un-
favorable outcome.
DIAGNOSTIC TESTING AND CLASSIFICATION
There is currently no reference standard for diagnosis of CTS,
which makes diagnostic confirmation challenging.
Some
patients will undergo EDX testing or diagnostic US, and in
some cases, findings will alter their course of treatment.
Electrodiagnostic testing provides an objective measure of
myelinated nerve fiber function relative to other nerves in
the hand and may differentiate CTS from other compression
neuropathies or nerve injuries. It provides measurements

of focal demyelination and axonal loss.
Electrodiagnostic
testing does not detect abnormalities in small, unmyelinated
nerve fiber function (C and A-
δ
), which are mediators of pain,
nor does it record sensory action potentials perceived by the
patient as paresthesia.

There are many ways to grade the severity of CTS based on
EDX test results.21 Many scales have been developed based
on nerve conduction, but currently there is no consensus
on a single scale to use for interpreting test results, and
authors have suggested there is a need to revisit existing
severity classifications.158 Some patients with CTS symptoms demonstrate normal EDX test results yet go on to
have statistical and clinically meaningful change in BCTQSSS and BCTQ-FSS following CTR.112

Diagnostic US is useful for detecting morphological changes in the median nerve and anatomical variations that may
be contributing to CTS pathogenesis. Measurements of
the median nerve cross-sectional area (CSA) at the carpal
tunnel inlet show the best reliability, validity, and diagnostic accuracy according to 2 recent systematic reviews.56,114
Diagnostic US can also detect an increase in the median
nerve CSA in pregnant women with a clinical diagnosis of
CTS72 and, according to a case series (n = 15), may be useful for differentiating cervical radiculopathy from CTS.43
Grading the severity of CTS using US has shown conflicting
evidence.152

Some patients will undergo surgical management, or
CTR for CTS. In the United States, over 500 000 CTR
surgeries are performed annually.58 One study on Medicare beneficiaries showed that surgical outcomes are
good, and there is a considerable amount of economic
benefit.82 The wait time for surgery in the United States,
reported in 1 small pilot study, was 12 days from decision to operate to CTR.31 However, wait times for surgery
in the other countries are considerably higher. Cheung
et al31 found the mean wait time in Canada was 147 days.
In Spain, the mean wait time was 355 days, with 1 of every 4 people waiting longer than 15 months.2 Long wait

SUMMARY
Although classic CTS has a typical symptom presentation,
the presence of neuropathic pain and extramedian symptom
spread can make diagnostic confirmation difficult. Patients
with atypical symptoms may require additional screening to
determine the site(s) of compression. There is also a need
for an accurate clinical tool to screen for central pain mechanisms in CTS. Based on the design of available studies on psychosocial factors, it is unclear if anxiety or depression were
present prior to CTS or vice versa. Nonetheless these may be
important areas for screening.

Some patients will undergo EDX testing and/or diagnostic
US, and performance of, or referral for additional diagnostic testing potentially may be under the purview of the
physical therapist. It is important to consider the additional
costs of these tests and whether results will potentially
alter the patient’s course of treatment, such as referral to
a surgeon. Carpal tunnel syndrome classification based
on clinical signs and symptoms is an important area for
future research that could guide therapists in their decision
making on whether to provide nonsurgical management
to a patient with CTS or refer the patient for a surgical
consultation. There are no high-quality, validated studies
confirming a point at which a patient undergoing a trial of
nonsurgical management should be referred for a surgical
consultation. The CPG development group recommends
that information in the subjective history combined with
data from objective tests and measures be used to
determine if a patient is appropriate for a trial of nonsurgical management. Factors for consideration include the
following:
(1) presence of thenar muscle atrophy (suggesting severe

CTS)
(2) symptom duration longer than 1 year
(3) history of a failed, prior nonsurgical intervention
(4) initial scores on the BCTQ-SSS greater than 2.5
(5) constant symptoms (night and day)
(6) degree of sensory impairment based on objective testing

chunks.text:
The use of forceful hand exertions, as measured by the Borg
Category-Ratio (CR-10), remains the strongest occupational risk factor for CTS.77 There is also moderate evidence
supporting increasing Strain Index as an occupational risk
factor.77 Strain Index is a measure of physical exposure to
frequency, duration, and intensity of movement, as well as
hand and wrist postures.67 High-quality evidence shows some

jobs, such as farming and manual labor,83,110 and manufacturing106 carry elevated risk for CTS. Recent studies on vibration exposure risk for CTS are conflicting.77,181,195 There was
no significant risk of CTS in job categories with low-force,
high-frequency computer keyboard work including secretaries, general office clerks, or receptionists and switchboard
operators.106

Results examining the interaction between sex and occupation are conflicting. Kraut et al106 found female workers had
more CTS cases compared to male workers within the same
job title, while other studies show that risk was comparable
in some occupational settings.83,110,171,178 Another study showed
greater risk for CTS in physically demanding work in individuals who were obese or overweight compared to those with
normal body weight.83

In summary, there are many potential risk factors for CTS.
Risk factors may contribute to the pathogenesis of CTS
through different anatomical or physiological changes within
the carpal tunnel or median nerve. For example, pathological
changes in patients with diabetes may be different than those
caused by occupational exertion. More research is needed to
examine the pathogenesis of CTS in the presence of different
risk factors.

The therapists’ examination for a patient with signs and
symptoms consistent with CTS serves multiple purposes.
First, the therapist should aim to differentiate between CTS
and conditions with similar presentations. Also, there is a
need to identify impairments in body structures and function, activity limitations, and participation restrictions. The
therapists’ examination should also identify concurrent
conditions or factors that might impact outcome, and ultimately, data from the examination should guide the therapist
in determining if the patient is a candidate for nonsurgical
management.

chunks.text:
The absence of a definitive reference standard complicates
confirming a CTS diagnosis. Thus, a compilation of data from
both the subjective history and objective examination should
be used in clinical decision making. The subjective examination should include a thorough history to gain understanding
of symptom characteristics, CTS risk factors, activity limitations, and participation restrictions. Medical, cervical, and
upper quarter screenings should be performed to rule out
serious medical pathology and proximal nerve lesions. It
is also important to screen the client for additional sites of
nerve compression since they can occur at multiple locations
while keeping in mind that CTS can refer into extramedian
territories.

The Examination section of this CPG organizes tests and
measures that aid in determining the presence or absence
of CTS and associated impairments in body structures and
function, ie, sensation and motor function. Specifically, this
section includes summaries on (1) hand diagrams and questionnaires used to gain information about the nature of the
patient’s symptoms, (2) provocative testing, (3) sensory and
motor testing, and (4) the use of test batteries or a combination of individual tests and measures. Tests and measures
of dexterity are provided under motor testing. Patient- or
self-reported measures of activity limitations and participation restrictions are discussed in the Outcome Measures section since these are the only valid instruments for assessing
change over time.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS AND SEVERITY MEASURES: HAND
DIAGRAMS AND QUESTIONNAIRES
Hand diagrams and questionnaires are patient self-report
measures used to assess the location and nature of the patient’s symptoms to aid in determining the CTS diagnosis.
There is evidence on 2 questionnaires: the Katz and Stirrat
hand symptom diagram (HSD)97 and the Kamath and Stothard questionnaire.94 The Katz and Stirrat HSD allows the

Examination

patient to give the location of their symptoms by shading
lined hand diagrams of the right and left hands and indicate
if symptoms include pain, numbness, tingling, or decreased
sensation. The likelihood of CTS based on the diagram is
rated as follows:
(1) Classic CTS: tingling, numbness, or decreased sensation

with or without pain in at least 2 of digits 1, 2, or 3;
symptoms in palm and dorsum of the hand excluded;
fifth-finger symptoms, wrist pain, or radiation proximal
to the wrist allowed;
(2) Probable CTS: same as classic CTS, except palmar symptoms are allowed unless confined solely to ulnar aspect;
(3) Possible CTS: tingling, numbness, decreased sensation,

and/or pain in at least 1 of digit 1, 2, or 3; and
(4) Unlikely CTS: no symptoms in digits 1, 2, or 3.97

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS AND SEVERITY MEASURES: HAND
DIAGRAMS AND QUESTIONNAIRES
Hand diagrams and questionnaires are patient self-report
measures used to assess the location and nature of the pa-
tient’s symptoms to aid in determining the CTS diagnosis.
There is evidence on 2 questionnaires: the Katz and Stirrat
hand symptom diagram (HSD)
and the Kamath and Sto-
thard questionnaire.
The Katz and Stirrat HSD allows the
Examination
patient to give the location of their symptoms by shading
lined hand diagrams of the right and left hands and indicate
if symptoms include pain, numbness, tingling, or decreased
sensation. The likelihood of CTS based on the diagram is
rated as follows:
(1)	 Classic CTS: tingling, numbness, or decreased sensation
with or without pain in at least 2 of digits 1, 2, or 3;
symptoms in palm and dorsum of the hand excluded;
fifth-finger symptoms, wrist pain, or radiation proximal
to the wrist allowed;
(2)	Probable CTS: same as classic CTS, except palmar symp-
toms are allowed unless confined solely to ulnar aspect;
(3)	Possible CTS: tingling, numbness, decreased sensation,
and/or pain in at least 1 of digit 1, 2, or 3; and
(4)	Unlikely CTS: no symptoms in digits 1, 2, or 3.

will be discussed in the Outcome Measures section due to
evidence supporting their use as outcome measures rather
than diagnostic instruments.

chunks.text:
In a systematic review of 12 studies examining tests
and measures used to screen workers for CTS, the
Katz and Stirrat HSD and the Kamath and Stothard
questionnaire had the best overall sensitivity and specificity
for diagnosing CTS when compared to the Phalen test, Tinel
sign, sensory and strength measures, and self-report questionnaires such as the BCTQ-SSS and BCTQ-FSS. For the Katz
and Stirrat HSD, sensitivity ranged from 34% to 93% and
specificity ranged from 25% to 84% (data pooled from 5 studies). For the Kamath and Stothard questionnaire, sensitivity
and specificity were 100% (based on data from 1 study).38

chunks.text:
Michigan Hand Outcomes Questionnaire
The MHQ is a 37-item hand-specific outcome measure with
6 subscales (overall hand function, ADLs, pain, work performance, aesthetics, and satisfaction). A total score or subscale
scores may be calculated out of 100 with higher scores indicating better hand performance. Scoring is complicated and
the MHQ must be licensed or used with permission.

Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®

Mahmood et al121 found the MHQ responsive in
patients (n = 101; age > 18 years; sex not reported)
who have undergone CTR surgery. The SRM increased with follow-up timing with the highest responsiveness at 6 weeks (1.17) and 3 months (1.26). At the 1-week
follow-up, the SRM was trace (0.06).

VAS average pain (n = 3434), and 17.60 for VAS during hand
function (n = 3481).

Evidence Synthesis
Nonsurgical Patients
Currently, patient self-reported outcome measures are the
most valid instruments for assessing change over time in
patients undergoing nonsurgical management for CTS, with
the BCTQ-SSS having the strongest evidence base. For this
revision, new data were available for the BCTQ-SSS, BCTQFSS, and VAS specific to those undergoing nonsurgical management. One study reported results of a secondary analysis
that combined surgical and nonsurgical patients and reported
MDIC scores for the BCTQ-SSS, BCTQ-FSS, and NPRS.
Threshold values for detecting a meaningful, clinically relevant change that have been reported are in TABLE 6.

Postsurgical Patients
Data specific to the surgically managed patient are now available for 3 domains of the PROMIS, MHQ, and QuickDASH.
The PROMIS-UE, PROMIS-PI, and MHQ are responsive
to change in patients undergoing CTR surgery; however, responsiveness of the BCTQ-SSS and BCTQ-FSS exceed those
of the PROMIS. The PROMIS-PF is neither valid nor responsive for measuring change following CTR surgery. While
the MHQ shows favorable results for assessing change, the
instrument is not readily available. Varying methods to calculate MCID or MIC produced a large range of estimates for the
BCTQ, PROMIS, and the QuickDASH in patients with CTS.

are slightly higher for those undergoing CTR surgery versus

Data specific to the surgically managed patient are now avail-

the MHQ shows favorable results for assessing change, the

BCTQ, PROMIS, and the QuickDASH in patients with CTS.

are slightly higher for those undergoing CTR surgery versus
those undergoing nonsurgical management.

Interpretation of intervention studies was challenged by the

For neural mobilization, this update includes 1 systematic review147 and 1 primary study.3 It also includes a meta-analysis85
and 1 primary study163 comparing carpal bone mobilization
with neural mobilization. The articles on neural mobilization
are conflicting. Authors of the systematic review concluded
that they cannot recommend using neural mobilization for patients with mild to moderate CTS,147 and in the primary study,3
the addition of hand and wrist-based differential tendon and
nerve gliding exercises for management of moderate-severity
CTS was equally as effective as an orthosis alone in the short
term (6 weeks) for improving BCTQ scores. Another study
showed that neural mobilization COM was more effective
than an orthosis alone or an orthosis combined with MLD.33
While short-term benefits are reported in some studies, a variety of techniques are being used, making it difficult to draw
a conclusion. No harms were reported for studies on nerve
tissue mobilization. There is conflicting evidence for the use
of neurodynamic mobilizations for management of mild- or
moderate-severity CTS, and no recommendation can be made.

MLD for short-term benefits of pain relief and symptom
severity was not superior to nerve glides or use of a wrist
orthoses. In studies on MLD, use of MLD was combined with
other interventions, making it difficult to draw a conclusion
about the use of MLD alone. No harms were reported for
studies on MLD. There is conflicting evidence for the use of
MLD for management of mild- or moderate-severity CTS,
and no recommendation can be made.

chunks.text:
Gaps in the Literature
There is a need for long-term, high-quality studies on different
manual therapy techniques in individuals with CTS. Studies
should provide interventions described in detail along with
the dosage. Also, there is a need for long-term, high-quality
studies on neural mobilization techniques that include valid
outcome measures and compare specific, reproducible neural
mobilization techniques to identify the most effective technique and appropriate dosage. Most studies that used tendon
and nerve gliding exercises are part of a multimodal approach,
obscuring the efficacy of these exercises alone. Studies should
include force, grade, direction, time, repetitions, etc, to improve the repeatability of the intervention. Additionally, there
is a need for long-term, high-quality studies on the use of MLD
in isolation for individuals with mild to moderate CTS. The
effectiveness of MLD in the studies reported33,92 is obscured
by using a multimodal approach, making it difficult to assess
the value of MLD as an intervention.

Authors of studies on nerve mobilization techniques should
provide more clarity in the use of neurodynamic techniques
described by Coppieters and Butler35 vs tendon and nerve

gliding techniques as described by Totten and Hunter.175
While both techniques are intended to improve nerve mobility, it is unclear as to whether 1 technique is better than the
other. Systematic reviews that pool data from studies using
ULNT techniques and nerve and tendon gliding exercises
described by Totten and Hunter175 may need to separate the
effects rather than combining data to provide clinicians with
more clarity on the benefit of each.

Previous studies found finger motions used when performing
tendon and nerve gliding described by Totten and Hunter175
affected the CSA and flattening ratios of the median nerve in
the carpal tunnel in both control participants and those with
CTS. The changes were more pronounced in participants
with CTS especially in the hook and fist positions, leading
authors to suggest these exercises could negatively impact the
median nerve through compression or strain.80,180 Coppieters
and Butler35 also measured the effect of nerve gliding at the
level of the wrist and digits, and concluded that the position
of the adjacent joints, especially the elbow, impacted the excursion and strain of the median nerve, suggesting tenodesis
exercises that include the elbow might be more effective than
isolated tendon and nerve glides. More research is needed to
determine the ideal positions for neural mobilization such
that mobility of the nerve is improved without additional
nerve compression or strain. Dynamic imaging studies with
tunnel pressure measurements and careful documentation of
proximal joint positioning during exercise may be helpful in
determining the effect of tendon and nerve gliding on CTS.

2026 Recommendations

median nerve through compression or strain.80,180 Coppieters
and Butler35 also measured the effect of nerve gliding at the
level of the wrist and digits, and concluded that the position
of the adjacent joints, especially the elbow, impacted the excursion and strain of the median nerve, suggesting tenodesis
exercises that include the elbow might be more effective than
isolated tendon and nerve glides. More research is needed to
determine the ideal positions for neural mobilization such
that mobility of the nerve is improved without additional
nerve compression or strain. Dynamic imaging studies with
tunnel pressure measurements and careful documentation of
proximal joint positioning during exercise may be helpful in
determining the effect of tendon and nerve gliding on CTS.

Gaps in the Literature
There is a need for long-term, high-quality studies on different
manual therapy techniques in individuals with CTS. Studies
should provide interventions described in detail along with
the dosage. Also, there is a need for long-term, high-quality
studies on neural mobilization techniques that include valid
outcome measures and compare specific, reproducible neural
mobilization techniques to identify the most effective technique and appropriate dosage. Most studies that used tendon
and nerve gliding exercises are part of a multimodal approach,
obscuring the efficacy of these exercises alone. Studies should
include force, grade, direction, time, repetitions, etc, to improve the repeatability of the intervention. Additionally, there
is a need for long-term, high-quality studies on the use of MLD
in isolation for individuals with mild to moderate CTS. The
effectiveness of MLD in the studies reported33,92 is obscured
by using a multimodal approach, making it difficult to assess
the value of MLD as an intervention.

Authors of studies on nerve mobilization techniques should
provide more clarity in the use of neurodynamic techniques
described by Coppieters and Butler35 vs tendon and nerve

gliding techniques as described by Totten and Hunter.175
While both techniques are intended to improve nerve mobility, it is unclear as to whether 1 technique is better than the
other. Systematic reviews that pool data from studies using
ULNT techniques and nerve and tendon gliding exercises
described by Totten and Hunter175 may need to separate the
effects rather than combining data to provide clinicians with
more clarity on the benefit of each.

with CTS especially in the hook and fist positions, leading

Evidence Update
There was no new evidence on therapeutic exercise.

journal of orthopaedic & sports physical therapy | volume 56 | number 4 | april 2026 | cpg29

In a double-blind RCT, authors investigated the
addition of KT to a multimodal therapy program
that included a prefabricated circumferential wrist
orthosis (KT), compared to the multimodal program and orthosis (ORT) or the multimodal program alone (CON).53
Forty-five participants (mean age: KT, 46.3 ± 9.2 years; CON,
47.2 ± 8.7 years; ORT, 49 ± 9.8 years; 53.3% female) with
EDX-confirmed bilateral, moderate-severity CTS were enrolled. For the KT group, tape was applied with 15% to 25%
tension using “space correction and buttonhole” techniques,
extending from the MCP joints to the humeral epicondyles
on the volar and dorsal surfaces of the hands, with a second
tape perpendicular and nearly circumferential around the
wrist. The tape was applied 5 days per week for 4 weeks and
worn overnight. The orthoses were worn nightly for 4 weeks.
All subjects attended therapy 5 times per week for 4 weeks
for a rehabilitation program, which consisted of moist heat
application for 15 minutes followed by pulsed US (1 MHz, 1:4
duty cycle, 1.0 W/cm2, gel coupling, 5 minutes per hand),
self-stretching as described by Sucher,168 tendon gliding exercises as described by Wehbe,183 nerve gliding exercises as
described by Totten and Hunter,175 a home exercise program
that included tendon and nerve gliding exercises, and instruction in activity modification. The home exercise program prescription was not reported. At 4 weeks, all groups
demonstrated statistically significant improvement in resting
and night pain VAS, BCTQ-SSS, and BCTQ-FSS scores
(P<.011). Between-group differences in changes scores
showed BCTQ-SSS scores favored KT over the ORT (MD,
−0.96; 95% CI: −1.11, −0.81; P<.001) and CON (MD, −1.13;
95% CI: −1.30, −0.96; P<.001). BCTQ-FSS scores also favored KT over the ORT (MD, −0.87; 95% CI: −1.11, −0.63;
P<.001) and CON (MD, −1.20; 95% CI: −1.47; −0.93;
P<.001). Pain VAS scores at rest also favored the KT group
over the ORT (MD, −1.2; 95% CI: −2.06, −0.34; P = .010)
and CON (MD, −1.4; 95% CI: −2.11, −0.69; P = .001) groups.
There was no significant difference in night pain between the
KT and ORT groups (MD, −0.6; 95% CI: −1.36, 0.16; P =
.191), but the difference between KT and CON was significant
(MD, −1.8; 95% CI: −2.84, −0.76; P = .004).53

off. Cupping was applied on the volar surface of the wrist over
the carpal tunnel using 50-mmHg suction for 5 minutes, followed by 2 minutes of progressing proximally on the forearm.
After 4 weeks, both groups made statistically significant and
clinically meaningful changes in pain VAS and BCTQ scores
(P<.001) The between-group analysis (controlled for pretreatment scores) showed a significant difference between groups
for the BCTQ-SSS scores (MD, 0.37; P<.001) and BCTQ-FSS
scores (MD, 0.63; P<.001), favoring cupping. There was no
significant difference between groups on pain VAS scores
(MD, 0.74; P = .085).132

Evidence Synthesis
According to 1 level II study, in the short and mid term, KT
plus exercise was superior to sham taping plus exercise in
participants with mild CTS for improving pain and symptom severity.42 There was conflicting evidence when authors
directly compared the addition of KT versus an orthosis to
a multimodal intervention for people with mild- or moderate-severity CTS. In women who were pregnant, cupping
was more effective than KT in the short term, although both
groups made meaningful improvements.132 In a single study54
included in the review by Karjalainen et al,96 the authors
found improved BCTQ scores following rigid tape application when compared to night orthosis use in the short term.
However, rigid taping is not included in the recommendations due to the low certainty of the evidence and risk of
bias. Application of KT and wearing schedules were heterogenous and without reported rationale. The mechanism for
the efficacy of taping also remains unclear and may be that
the presence of the tape reduced functional use of the hand
through proprioceptive input, motion restriction, or efforts to
protect the application between sessions. None of the studies
reported adverse effects.

Gaps in Knowledge
To determine the effectiveness of taping for CTS, high-quality
studies are needed with true controls, larger samples, and
longer-term follow-up, evaluating the efficacy of both KT and
rigid taping as single interventions using validated outcome
measures; identifying the optimal tape configuration, dosage,
and length of wear; and comparing their effectiveness to other nonsurgical CTS interventions for the short and long term.

2026 Recommendation

through proprioceptive input, motion restriction, or efforts to
protect the application between sessions. None of the studies
reported adverse effects.

Gaps in Knowledge
To determine the effectiveness of taping for CTS, high-quality
studies are needed with true controls, larger samples, and
longer-term follow-up, evaluating the efficacy of both KT and
rigid taping as single interventions using validated outcome
measures; identifying the optimal tape configuration, dosage,
and length of wear; and comparing their effectiveness to other nonsurgical CTS interventions for the short and long term.

2026 Recommendation

Evidence Synthesis
According to 1 level II study, in the short and mid term, KT
plus exercise was superior to sham taping plus exercise in
participants with mild CTS for improving pain and symp-
tom severity.
There was conflicting evidence when authors
directly compared the addition of KT versus an orthosis to
a multimodal intervention for people with mild- or moder-
ate-severity CTS. In women who were pregnant, cupping
was more effective than KT in the short term, although both
groups made meaningful improvements.
In a single study
included in the review by Karjalainen et al,
the authors
found improved BCTQ scores following rigid tape applica-
tion when compared to night orthosis use in the short term.
However, rigid taping is not included in the recommenda-
tions due to the low certainty of the evidence and risk of
bias. Application of KT and wearing schedules were heter-
ogenous and without reported rationale. The mechanism for
the efficacy of taping also remains unclear and may be that
the presence of the tape reduced functional use of the hand
through proprioceptive input, motion restriction, or efforts to
protect the application between sessions. None of the studies
reported adverse effects.
Gaps in Knowledge
To determine the effectiveness of taping for CTS, high-quality
studies are needed with true controls, larger samples, and
longer-term follow-up, evaluating the efficacy of both KT and
rigid taping as single interventions using validated outcome
measures; identifying the optimal tape configuration, dosage,
and length of wear; and comparing their effectiveness to oth-
er nonsurgical CTS interventions for the short and long term.
2026 Recommendation
